There is a particular moment in late afternoon when the light begins to fail, and the world seems to hold its breath. It is not yet dusk, but the sharp edges of things soften, as if the air itself is taking a long, slow exhale. This is the threshold hour. I think we live most of our lives in such in-between spaces, though we rarely notice them.

The pause between one heartbeat and the next. The silence after a sentence is spoken but before it is understood. The cool slide of water as it moves over pebbles in a stream, never stopping, never quite the same. We are creatures of thresholds, standing on the porch of a house we cannot enter, looking back at the door we just closed.

Perhaps that is why I love the first snowfall in early winter. It arrives as a quiet surprise, a covering that erases the sharp geometry of the yard and turns familiar noises into muffled whispers. The world becomes a page half-written, waiting. It is not yet deep winter, and autumn still lingers in the scent of woodsmoke. But the threshold has been crossed.

Maybe wisdom is nothing more than learning to linger in these passages, to feel the hinge of the door between what was and what will be. The light fails, and I let it. Tomorrow will arrive on its own.
